Construction Contracts under Saudi Law

Mutual Obligations, Liability, and Performance Disputes

Construction contracts are among the most important commercial contracts in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia because of their direct connection with construction, engineering projects, and infrastructure. They are among the contracts most frequently brought before commercial courts due to delay, defective performance, or disputes concerning payment certificates and instalments.

This article provides a precise and comprehensive legal analysis of construction contracts, addressing the mutual obligations of the contractor and employer, statutory liability, the principal disputes arising during performance, and practical recommendations for protecting rights.

Legal Overview: The Framework Governing Construction Contracts.

Construction contracts in the Kingdom are regulated by the general rules on contracts and obligations in the Civil Transactions Law, including provisions on contractual liability, compensation, and liquidated damages. Evidentiary disputes are subject to the Evidence Law, particularly its rules on burden of proof, written and digital evidence, inspection, and expert evidence. Commercial disputes, or those arising between merchants as applicable, are heard by commercial courts under the Commercial Courts Law and its Implementing Regulations, having regard to the nature of the parties and subject matter.

First: Nature of the Construction Contract.

A construction contract is an agreement under which a contractor undertakes to perform specified work—usually engineering or construction work—in return for a defined fee paid by the employer. It is characterized by the following:

Legally, this contract is based on one party's obligation to complete work or deliver a specified result for consideration, making it binding on both parties: the contractor must perform as agreed, while the employer must pay and enable performance. General rules on contractual validity, good-faith performance, and the consequences of breach apply.

  • It depends on the final result of the work rather than mere effort

  • It includes detailed technical specifications

  • It is often linked to a defined schedule

  • It requires technical supervision by the employer or a consultant

Second: Mutual Obligations of Contractor and Employer.

1) Contractor Obligations:

The contractor must:

  • Perform work according to approved technical specifications

  • Comply with the schedule

  • Provide necessary labour and equipment

  • Comply with occupational safety standards

  • Remedy apparent and latent defects

  • Deliver the project in its agreed condition

2) Employer Obligations:

The employer must:

  • Pay instalments when due

  • Provide and hand over the site to the contractor

  • Provide drawings and technical documents

  • Remove obstacles preventing performance

  • Issue change orders when required

  • Accept the work after inspection

Third: Essential Terms of Construction Contracts.

1) Scope of Work

It must be precisely defined and include:

  • Drawings

  • Technical specifications

  • Materials used

  • Performance stages

2) Schedule

It is one of the most important terms and must include:

  • Work commencement date

  • Performance stages

  • Final handover date

  • Delay penalties

3) Payment Certificates and Instalments

The following must be specified:

  • Method for calculating payment certificates

  • Payment dates

  • Advance payments

  • Bank guarantees

4) Liquidated Damages Clause

It commonly applies in cases of:

  • Delay in completion

  • Defective performance

  • Non-compliance with specifications

Under the Civil Transactions Law, a liquidated damages clause is a form of agreed compensation: the parties may assess compensation in advance for non-performance or delay. Entitlement is not absolute; the court may reduce it if excessive or if the obligation has been partly performed, and it is not due if no damage is proven.

5) Change Orders (Variation Orders)

They govern:

  • Additional work

  • Omitted work

  • Price adjustments

  • Extension of time

Fourth: Liability in Construction Contracts.

1) Contractor Liability

The contractor is responsible for:

  • Technical defects

  • Unjustified delay

  • Breach of specifications

  • Damage arising from negligence or poor performance

This liability is governed by contractual liability rules. If the contractor breaches a material obligation in the contract, specifications, or schedule, the employer may seek performance, rectification, or compensation, as appropriate, if breach, damage, and causation are established, unless an external cause, force majeure, or contributory fault by the employer exists.

2) Employer Liability

The employer may be liable if it:

  • Delays payment of payment certificates

  • Fails to hand over the site on time

  • Issues change orders without extending the performance period

  • Provides inaccurate drawings

The employer's breach of its corresponding obligations may wholly or partly release the contractor from the consequences of delay, or entitle it to request an extension of time or compensation, especially where delay results from failure to hand over the site, delayed approval of drawings, or change orders affecting the scope or duration without clear contractual treatment.

Fifth: Key Construction Contract Disputes.

Disputes commonly arise in:

  • Delay in completion

  • Disputes over payment certificates

  • Defective performance

  • Unapproved additional work

  • Latent defects after handover

  • Contract termination and project withdrawal

These disputes are among the matters most frequently brought before commercial courts.

Sixth: Saudi Judicial Approach to Construction Disputes.

In light of the general principles of the Civil Transactions Law and Evidence Law, construction disputes demonstrate a practical judicial approach that examines the contract, technical documents, correspondence, and expert reports rather than relying on mere allegations or abstract estimates, including:

  • Holding the contractor liable for liquidated damages in cases of unjustified delay

  • Accepting technical expert reports as strong evidence in technical disputes

  • Ordering the employer to pay where work completion to specification is established

  • Rejecting undocumented claims such as unapproved additional work

  • Precisely determining liability based on documents and technical correspondence

Seventh: Proving Construction Contract Disputes.

Courts rely on:

  • Handover and acceptance records

  • Payment certificates

  • Technical correspondence

  • Consultant reports

  • Photographs and videos

  • Expert testimony

  • Change orders

  • Contracts and appendices

The general rules of the Evidence Law provide that the burden of proof lies with the claimant and that facts to be proved must be relevant, material, and admissible. Written documents, electronic correspondence, meeting minutes, digital evidence, and expert reports are therefore especially important in proving the scope of completed work, the cause of delay, and entitlement to payments or compensation.

Technical reports are among the strongest forms of evidence in this type of dispute.

Technical expertise in this type of action is not a substitute for evidence, but a means of helping the court understand technical issues relating to quality of performance, completion percentages, defects, and causes of delay. The court retains discretion to assess an expert report in light of its methodology, documents, and the parties' objections.

Eighth: Practical Recommendations for a Strong Construction Contract.

For strong legal protection, it is advisable to:

  • Precisely define the scope of work

  • Set a clear schedule

  • Include a liquidated damages clause

  • Document every performance stage

  • Approve change orders in writing

· Expressly state the mechanism for extending time and the effect of change orders on the liquidated damages clause

  • Engage an independent engineering consultant

  • Retain all technical correspondence

· Specify jurisdiction, an arbitration clause, or amicable settlement consistently with applicable laws

Construction contracts are among the most sensitive and complex contracts in the Saudi market and require precise drafting and sound technical and legal management. Proper legal grounding in civil transactions, evidence, and commercial jurisdiction strengthens the parties' legal positions, reduces disputes, and facilitates their determination in court. The clearer the obligations, the better documented the records, and the more defined the schedule, the fewer disputes arise and the stronger both parties' protection before the courts.

Notice: This article is for general legal awareness purposes and does not replace specialized legal advice based on the facts of each case.

blogs.bodyEn:
Commercial Agency Contracts in the Saudi Legal System

The Rights and Responsibilities of the Agent and Principal

Commercial agencies are influential regulatory instruments in the Saudi market, enabling businesses to expand through authorized agents within a defined geographic or sectoral scope. The relationship is governed by the Commercial Agencies Law, its Implementing Regulations, and related laws. Precise drafting becomes particularly important where exclusivity, sales obligations, or trademark-use rights are involved, as breaches may result in disputes and compensation.

This article provides a focused legal overview of commercial agency contracts in the Kingdom. It reviews the rights of agents and principals, explains their mutual obligations, highlights the principal forms of dispute brought before the commercial courts, and offers practical recommendations to reduce risk and protect contractual interests.

First: The Nature of a Commercial Agency Contract.

A commercial agency contract is an agreement authorizing the agent to represent the principal in marketing or selling its products, or providing its services, within a specified scope and under contractual and legal controls governing the parties’ relationship.

This contract has several key characteristics, including:

  • It is based on commercial representation

  • It is commonly associated with a trademark or a specific product

  • It includes marketing and operational obligations

  • It is governed by the Commercial Agencies Law and its Implementing Regulations

Second: The Legal Framework for Commercial Agencies in Saudi Arabia.

Commercial agencies in the Kingdom are subject to a range of relevant legal frameworks, foremost among them:

  • Commercial Agencies Law

  • Implementing Regulations of the Commercial Agencies Law

  • Anti-Commercial Fraud Law

  • Trademarks Law

  • Judicial precedents of the commercial courts

Registering the agency with the Ministry of Commerce is an important legal requirement for establishing the relationship and regulating its effects before the competent authorities. It also helps limit disputes concerning the agent’s status and the scope of the agency.

Third: The Principal’s Rights under a Commercial Agency Contract.

The principal has several rights that enable it to monitor implementation of the agency and protect its commercial interests, most notably:

  • The right to supervise the agent’s performance

  • The right to set prices and marketing policies

  • The right to terminate the agency in accordance with the contract terms

  • The right to protect the trademark from misuse

  • The right to request periodic reports on sales and inventory

Depending on the contract terms and the circumstances surrounding the relationship, the principal may also seek rescission or termination of the contract where the agent commits a material breach.

Fourth: The Commercial Agent’s Rights.

Conversely, the commercial agent has essential rights that enable it to perform its role and protect its investments, including:

  • The right to exclusive distribution within the agreed geographic scope

  • The right to receive products or services on fair terms

  • The right to compensation where the agency is terminated without legitimate cause

  • The right to use the trademark within the scope of the agency

  • The right to receive technical and marketing support from the principal

Courts may award compensation where it is established that the agency was terminated without legitimate cause and the agent suffered direct damage as a result, taking into account the contract terms, documents, and circumstances surrounding the relationship.

These rights are matched by reciprocal obligations: the principal’s right to supervision and reports corresponds to the agent’s obligation of disclosure and documentation, while the agent’s right to support and exclusivity corresponds to the principal’s obligation not to breach the agreed scope.

Fifth: The Principal’s Obligations.

The principal’s principal obligations include:

  • Providing products or services at the agreed quality

  • Supporting the agent technically and in marketing

  • Not dealing with other agents within the scope of an exclusive agency

  • Observing agreed prices and policies

  • Remedying defects or technical problems in products

Sixth: The Agent’s Obligations.

Correspondingly, the agent bears essential obligations, most notably:

  • Marketing products in accordance with the specified standards

  • Maintaining the reputation of the trademark

·         Providing after-sales services where the nature of the products requires it, including warranty, maintenance, spare parts, and customer service, in accordance with the contract and relevant laws and without prejudice to consumer rights or the trademark’s reputation.

  • Complying with prices and marketing policies

  • Submitting periodic reports to the principal

  • Not selling competing products if the agency is exclusive

Seventh: Principal Disputes in Commercial Agency Contracts.

Disputes in commercial agency contracts commonly arise from unclear obligations, weak documentation, or differences between the parties in interpreting the scope of the agency. Their principal forms include:

  • Terminating the agency without legitimate cause

  • The agent’s failure to meet sales quotas

  • Misuse of the trademark

  • Delay in supplying products

  • Disagreement over compensation upon contract termination

  • Dealing with unauthorized agents within the agency’s scope

For example, an agent may invest in showrooms, inventory, and sales teams based on an exclusive agency, only for the principal to end the relationship without adequate notice or appoint another agent within the same scope. A dispute may also arise when the agent sells competing products or uses the trademark beyond the authorized limits.

These disputes are particularly important because of their direct connection to the agent’s investments, the trademark’s reputation, and the stability of the commercial relationship between the parties.

Eighth: Termination and Compensation in Commercial Agency Contracts.

When an agency is terminated, the inquiry is not limited to the existence of a contractual provision permitting termination; it also extends to the manner in which that right was exercised, the notice period, the reason for termination, the scale of the agent’s investments, the extent to which sales targets were achieved, and the nature of proven direct damages. The contract should therefore include a clear mechanism for notice and cure before rescission, and specified criteria for assessing compensation for wrongful termination.

Ninth: Saudi Judicial Approach to Agency Disputes.

In commercial agency disputes, the commercial judiciary considers the contract terms, the nature of the relationship, exchanged documents, and the extent to which breach and damage are established. Applications that may arise in this context include:

·         Awarding compensation against the principal where termination without legitimate cause and damage are established

·         Protecting the exclusive agent where a breach of the exclusivity scope or unfair competition is established

·         Awarding compensation against the agent where misuse of the trademark or exceeding the scope of the licence is established

  • Rejecting undocumented claims

  • Relying on commercial records and correspondence to establish the breach

Tenth: Essential Clauses in a Commercial Agency Contract.

A commercial agency contract is stronger when it includes clear clauses defining the scope of the relationship and anticipating potential areas of dispute. The most important clauses include:

·         Precisely identifying the parties and their legal capacities

·         Defining the geographic and subject-matter scope of the agency

·         Stating the extent and limits of exclusivity and the effects of breaching it

·         Specifying the contract term and the mechanism for renewal or non-renewal

·         Setting sales targets and supply and payment terms

·         Regulating use of the trademark and marketing materials

·         Specifying warranty, maintenance, and after-sales service obligations

·         Regulating periodic reports, confidentiality, and non-compete obligations

·         Specifying mechanisms for termination, rescission, compensation, and dispute resolution

Eleventh: Practical Recommendations for Drafting a Strong Agency Contract.

To achieve more effective contractual protection, it is not advisable to rely solely on a standard contract template. The contract should instead be tailored to the nature of the product, the scale of investment, the scope of exclusivity, warranty and maintenance obligations, and the supply and payment mechanism. It is also recommended to document commercial correspondence, register the agency with the Ministry of Commerce, and carefully use the terms termination, rescission, and non-renewal in a manner consistent with the reason for the relationship’s end and its effects.

Commercial agency contracts are a central instrument for expansion in the Saudi market, but they require particular care in defining scope, exclusivity, obligations, and termination and compensation mechanisms. The better documented and registered the contractual relationship is, and the more it is supported by clear correspondence and performance reports, the lower the likelihood of disputes and the greater the protection of the agent’s and principal’s interests. Accordingly, specialist legal review before signing or renewal remains essential, particularly where substantial investments, exclusive rights, or a trademark-use licence are involved.

Notice: This article is for awareness purposes only and does not constitute legal advice.

blogs.bodyEn:
Proving Contracts Before the Saudi Courts

Evidence, Presumptions, Evidentiary Value of Documents, and Digital Evidence

Proving contracts is among the most important stages of litigation in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as the judge bases the ruling on the evidence presented, not on personal knowledge. With the issuance of the Saudi Evidence Law and the subsequent Procedural Guide to the Evidence Law, rules of evidence have become clearer and more organized, enhancing confidence in commercial and civil transactions.

This article focuses on proving contracts from a practical perspective: how a litigant can prove the existence, performance, or breach of a contract, and which documents strengthen the litigant's position before the court.

1. The Legal Framework for Proving Contracts in Saudi Arabia:

Evidence in the Kingdom is governed by several legislative and judicial sources, foremost among them the Saudi Evidence Law issued by Royal Decree No. M/43, dated 26/5/1443 AH, the related judicial rules and procedures, and the established judicial practice of the competent courts.

  • Saudi Evidence Law issued by Royal Decree No. (M/43)

  • Procedural Guide to the Evidence Law issued by Minister of Justice Decision No. (921)

  • Judicial precedents of commercial and civil courts

The Law confirms that the judge does not rule based on personal knowledge, but rather on valid evidence presented that is relevant to the dispute.

2. The Basic Rule of Evidence:

The general rule is that whoever asserts a right or a fact material to the dispute bears the burden of proving it. If that party fails to provide sufficient evidence, the opposing party may deny the claim, and the court may resort to an oath where provided for by law.

3. Types of Evidence in Proving Contracts:

The Law sets out methods of proof in clear chapters, the most important of which are:

3.1 Admission:

An admission is one of the strongest means of proof because it entails the opposing party's acknowledgment of the right claimed, provided it is validly made by a person authorized to make such an admission. Its evidentiary value depends on its scope and legal conditions.

3.2 Writing - Documents:

They are divided into:

  • Official documents: such as notarized contracts and instruments; these are the strongest evidence.

  • Private documents: contracts between the parties, invoices, and correspondence.

3.3 Digital Evidence:

This includes:

  • Electronic messages

  • Digital records

  • Digital signature

  • Electronic system logs (Logs)

The Law recognizes digital evidence as an accepted means of proof.

3.4 Testimony:

It is admissible subject to specific conditions, particularly in transactions that do not exceed a certain value, whereas writing is required for major financial transactions.

3.5 Presumptions:

They involve inferring an unknown fact from a known fact and are considered supporting evidence.

3.6 Oath:

It is divided into:

  • Decisive oath: resolves the dispute.

  • Supplementary oath: completes incomplete evidence.

3.7 Expert Evidence and Inspection:

The court resorts to experts in technical matters, particularly in commercial and construction contracts.

4. Evidentiary Value of Documents in Proving Contracts:

4.1 Evidentiary Value of Official Documents:

They carry full evidentiary force unless challenged for forgery. A forgery challenge is an independent procedure governed by clear provisions in the Law.

4.2 Evidentiary Value of Private Documents:

They are admissible if they are:

  • issued by the party

  • signed or sealed

  • not denied, or their authenticity has been established through technical expertise

4.3 Evidentiary Value of Digital Evidence:

The Law requires that it be:

  • attributable

  • tamper-proof

  • issued by a trusted system

  • connected to the fact in dispute

5. Burden of Proof and Conflicting Evidence:

The Law provides that the court:

  • determines the burden of proof before taking evidence

  • does not prevent a party from presenting evidence except pursuant to a legal provision

  • may rely on incomplete evidence if supported by other evidence or a presumption

  • states the reasons for preferring one item of evidence over another where they conflict

6. When Is Writing Required to Prove a Contract?

Under the Evidence Law:

  • The general rule is freedom of proof

·         However, financial transactions exceeding SAR 100,000 are generally not proved by witness testimony alone, unless a provision or exception permits this. Therefore, writing remains the safest means for high-value contracts.

7. Practical Recommendations for Proving Contracts Before the Courts:

To ensure the strength of your legal position, it is recommended to:

  • document contracts in writing

  • preserve electronic correspondence

  • use an approved digital signature

  • retain invoices and delivery records

  • document any amendment or subsequent agreement

  • engage a technical expert for technical contracts

  • present evidence in a logical order reflecting the sequence of facts

Proving contracts before the Saudi courts depends on the quality, integrity, and connection of evidence to the facts in dispute, not on the judge's personal knowledge or a mere allegation. The more systematically contracts, correspondence, appendices, and invoices are retained, and the more capable digital evidence is of attribution and verification, the stronger the rights holder's legal position and the greater the court's ability to form its conviction. Accordingly, careful documentation from the outset of the contractual relationship is an important preventive measure to reduce disputes and protect rights in litigation.

blogs.bodyEn:
Commercial Supply Contracts in Saudi Arabia

Key Legal Clauses and Risks of Breach

Supply contracts are among the most common contracts in the Saudi market, particularly in the construction, industrial, commercial, and logistics sectors. They are the legal framework governing the relationship between the supplier and the customer and defining the obligations relating to the delivery of goods, materials, or equipment in accordance with specified specifications and agreed deadlines.

This article helps business owners, procurement managers, and legal advisers understand the clauses that should not be overlooked in supply contracts and how to reduce the risks of delay, non-conformity, and commercial disputes before the Saudi courts.

As commercial projects expand and transaction volumes rise, it becomes increasingly important to structure supply contracts carefully to avoid disputes relating to delays, non-conformity with specifications, or breaches of obligations. This article therefore provides a legal review of the key contractual clauses, the risks of breach, and the principal practical considerations in dealing with this type of contract.

Supply contracts are particularly important in Saudi Arabia because they combine commercial obligations, risk management, and the assurance of project continuity, making precise drafting an essential element in protecting both the supplier and the customer from potential disputes.

First: The Nature of a Commercial Supply Contract:

A supply contract is an agreement under which the supplier undertakes to deliver materials, goods, or equipment to the customer, either in a single delivery or in periodic instalments, in return for an agreed price or financial consideration, in accordance with the specifications, deadlines, and delivery conditions set out in the contract.

This contract is characterised by the following:

  • It is based on repeated or phased delivery

  • It is often connected with commercial or industrial projects

  • It requires precise specifications for the materials or products

  • It requires a clear delivery schedule

Second: Essential Clauses in Supply Contracts:

1) Precise Description of Materials or Products:

The contract must include:

  • Technical specifications

  • Required quality

  • Applicable standards

  • Country of origin

  • Inspection and testing methods

The more precise the description, the lower the likelihood of a dispute over conformity.

2) Delivery Schedule:

This is one of the most important clauses relied upon by the commercial courts and should include:

  • Date of each instalment

  • Place of delivery

  • Transport and storage conditions

  • Responsibility for delay

3) Price and Payment Mechanism:

It is preferable to specify:

  • Total price

  • Unit price

  • Payment terms

  • Advance payments

  • Financial guarantees (if any)

4) Liquidated Damages Clause:

This is an essential clause in supply contracts and applies in the event of:

  • Delay in delivery

  • Non-conformity with specifications

  • Refusal to deliver

5) Inspection and Acceptance of Materials:

The contract should provide for:

  • Inspection period

  • Objection mechanism

  • Liability for apparent and latent defects

6) Force Majeure:

To define the circumstances in which the supplier is relieved of liability, such as:

  • Natural disasters

  • Logistical crises

  • Emergency government decisions

Third: Principal Forms of Breach in Supply Contracts:

Disputes commonly arise from:

  • Delay in delivery

  • Delivery of materials that do not conform to specifications

  • Partial delivery without justification

  • Refusal to deliver after receiving payments

  • Defects in materials appearing after use

These are among the most common types of cases brought before the commercial courts.

Fourth: Saudi Judicial Approach to Supply Disputes:

In many supply disputes, commercial courts consider the clarity of the contractual obligations, proof of delay or non-conformity, and the existence of supporting documents such as purchase orders, delivery records, and technical expert reports.

  • Holding the supplier liable for liquidated damages in the event of delay or non-conformity

  • Accepting technical expert reports as strong evidence in disputes concerning specifications

  • Ordering the supplier to pay compensation where the breach causes harm to the project

  • Rejecting undocumented excuses such as unproven logistical excuses

  • Protecting the party acting in good faith, particularly where the documents are clear

Fifth: Methods of Proving Breach in Supply Contracts:

The courts rely on the following evidence:

  • Invoices

  • Purchase orders

  • Delivery and receipt records

  • Commercial correspondence

  • Technical inspection reports

  • Payment records

  • Photographs and videos

  • Expert testimony

Electronic correspondence may be important evidence of delay or non-conformity where it can be linked to the contractual relationship and its source, content, and context can be established.

Sixth: Risks of Breach in Supply Contracts:

Breach may result in:

  • Project stoppage or disruption

  • Direct financial losses

  • Loss of customers or related contracts

  • Lengthy legal disputes

  • Application of the liquidated damages clause

  • A claim for compensation against the supplier

Seventh: Practical Recommendations for Drafting a Strong Supply Contract:

To ensure strong legal protection, it is recommended to:

  • Define technical specifications precisely

  • Set a clear and detailed delivery schedule

  • Include a liquidated damages clause

  • Provide for an inspection and acceptance mechanism

  • Document every delivery instalment in an official record

  • Use reliable contract management platforms

  • Engage a technical expert for major contracts

Note: This article provides a general overview of the principal legal aspects of commercial supply contracts and is not a substitute for specialised legal advice that takes into account the facts, documents, and circumstances of performance of each contract.

Frequently Asked Questions About Commercial Supply Contracts:

What is the most important clause in a supply contract?
The description of materials, the delivery schedule, and the inspection mechanism are among the most important clauses because they define the standard for performance and make it easier to prove breach in a dispute.

When is a supplier considered in breach of contract?
A breach commonly occurs in the event of unjustified delay, delivery of non-conforming materials, refusal to deliver, or violation of the inspection and acceptance conditions.

Is a liquidated damages clause alone sufficient to secure compensation?
A liquidated damages clause is important, but its application is affected by its drafting, proof of breach and harm, and the circumstances surrounding contract performance.

Supply contracts are among the most important commercial contracts in the Saudi market and require precise drafting that protects both parties and limits disputes before they arise. The clearer the specifications, the more defined the schedules, and the better documented the inspection and acceptance mechanism, the greater the prospects of smooth contract performance and stronger trust between the supplier and the customer.

blogs.excerptEn: Syrian law distinguishes between consensual, formal, and real contracts because each type has different requirements for formation and legal effect.
blogs.seoDescriptionEn: Understand consensual, formal, and real contracts under Syrian law, including formation, validity, delivery, registration, and legal effects.
blogs.bodyEn:
Consensual, Formal, and Real Contracts in Syrian Law

A Simplified Study of Contract Formation and Its Legal Effects

IContracts constitute the fundamental legal framework through which civil and commercial transactions are organized. They are the means by which obligations arise and by which the parties’ rights and duties are defined. However, the validity of a contract and its effects do not always depend merely on the existence of an agreement between the contracting parties. In certain cases, the law may require compliance with a particular form or the actual delivery of the subject matter of the contract in order for its formation to be complete or for it to produce its legal effect.

This gives rise to the distinction between consensual, formal, and real contracts, a distinction with a direct practical effect because it helps determine the moment a contract is formed, the conditions for its validity, the extent to which it is effective between the contracting parties or against third parties, and the legal means necessary to prove it in the event of a dispute.

This classification is particularly important in Syrian law, especially in transactions involving in rem rights in immovable property, real securities, or contracts addressed by special provisions of the Civil Code.

Introduction: The Meaning of Classifying Contracts According to Their Method of Formation.

This classification identifies the element legally required for a contract to be fully formed. The general rule is that a contract is based on consent; however, the legislator may depart from that rule through a special provision and make form or delivery an essential element or a necessary procedure for certain effects to arise.

  • Consensual contracts.

  • Formal contracts.

  • Real contracts.

When dealing with any contract, it is not enough to consider its name alone; reference must be made to its legal nature and to the special provisions governing it. A contract may be consensual in principle yet, in a particular form, be subject to a special form or procedure.

First: Consensual Contracts.

A consensual contract is formed upon the mere concurrence of the contracting parties’ wills on its essential elements, through a definite offer and a corresponding acceptance, without the need for a special form or delivery, unless the law provides otherwise.

This type represents the general rule in the general theory of contract because the principle of freedom of contract presumes, within its legal limits, that consent is sufficient to create an obligation when capacity, subject matter, cause, and all other general conditions prescribed by law are present.

Examples of consensual contracts:

  • A contract for the sale of movable property.

  • A service contract.

  • A consultancy contract.

  • Supply contracts.

  • An employment contract.

  • An agency contract.

These examples remain subject to any special provision that may require writing, authentication, or a particular procedure for purposes of proof, regulation, or effectiveness, without necessarily changing the nature of the contract unless the law makes form an essential requirement for formation or validity.

The legal significance of consensual contracts:

The consensual nature of a contract does not mean that writing has no effect. Although writing is not a condition for formation in most consensual contracts, it remains an essential means of proving the contract’s existence and determining its content and terms, especially where a dispute arises concerning the scope of obligations, the amount of consideration, the contract term, or conditions for its termination.

Second: Formal Contracts:

A formal contract is one for which the law does not consider consent alone sufficient, but requires a particular form or procedure—such as an official instrument, writing, authentication, or registration—in order to complete its formation, validity, or effectiveness, as determined by the legal provision governing the transaction.

This form may consist of:

  • Drawing up the contract in writing.

  • Authenticating it before the competent authority.

  • Registering it in official registers.

  • Completing any procedure required by law.

A distinction must be drawn here between form as a condition for formation or validity, the absence of which results in the non-existence or nullity of the contract, and form as a condition for effectiveness or enforceability against third parties, where the transaction may remain valid between its parties but not produce certain effects until the required procedure is completed.

Examples of formal contracts:

Among the most prominent practical applications in Syrian law are transactions involving in rem rights in immovable property, since the transfer or acquisition of such rights is generally linked to entry in the land register under the governing provisions. Certain forms of mortgage and transactions that the law requires to be authenticated or registered in order to produce their full legal effects also fall within this framework.

Accordingly, failure to register where registration is required by law may not be a mere minor formal defect; rather, it may affect the transfer or effectiveness of the right, or the ability to invoke it, depending on the nature of the right and transaction and on the applicable provision.

Why does the law require form in some contracts?

The legislator requires form in certain cases to achieve several objectives, most importantly:

  • Protecting contracting parties from haste or fraud.

  • Reducing disputes.

  • Ensuring stability in transactions.

  • Protecting the rights of third parties.

  • Ensuring the integrity of official registers.

Third: Real Contracts:

A real contract is one whose formation is not complete upon consent alone but requires, in addition to the concurrence of wills, delivery of the subject matter of the contract or transfer of its possession in the manner prescribed by law. In this type, delivery is not merely performance of an obligation arising from the contract; rather, it is an element necessary for the existence of the contract itself in cases where the law or legal scholarship regards it as an essential element of formation.

Thus, delivery in a real contract differs from delivery in a consensual contract: in the former, it is required for formation; in the latter, it may be merely an obligation resulting from a contract previously formed by consent.

Examples of real contracts:

Examples traditionally cited in legal scholarship as real contracts, subject to the special provisions applicable to each contract, include:

  • A loan for use.

  • A loan.

  • A deposit contract.

  • A possessory pledge in cases where the law requires transfer of possession.

In every case, the special provisions of the Syrian Civil Code must be consulted, because classifying a contract as real or consensual may be affected by its nature, the purpose of delivery, and the provisions the legislator has prescribed for it.

Practical example:

If one person agrees with another to lend that person a sum of money at a later date, the agreement alone may not be sufficient to establish a loan contract as a real contract in situations where delivery is required. Rather, the contract is completed when the amount is actually delivered to the borrower. The prior agreement to deliver may, depending on its wording and circumstances, raise the issue of a promise to contract or an obligation to conclude the contract in the future.

Why is this classification important?

The importance of this classification appears in numerous legal issues, including:

  • Determining whether the contract was validly formed.

  • Knowing when contractual obligations arise.

  • Determining the appropriate means of proof.

  • Clarifying the rights and obligations incumbent on each party.

  • Determining whether the nullity or ineffectiveness of the contract may be invoked.

An error in characterizing the contract or an omission of the required form, delivery, or registration may lead to serious legal consequences, such as inability to prove a right, failure to transfer it, inability to invoke it against third parties, or nullity of the transaction in cases where the procedure is an essential requirement.

The distinction between formation, validity, proof, and effectiveness:

It is important not to confuse contract formation, validity, proof, and effectiveness. A contract may be formed by consent alone but require writing to prove it in a dispute. A contract may be valid between its parties yet not be effective against third parties until registration or completion of a particular legal procedure. Likewise, the absence of an essential element of the contract or one of its fundamental conditions may lead to nullity, whereas failure to complete a procedure prescribed for enforceability may only result in the transaction being ineffective against third parties.

Legal advice before concluding any contract:

Before signing any contract, the following is recommended:

  • Verify whether the law requires a particular form for the contract.

  • Complete all required formal procedures.

  • Confirm whether delivery is a condition for formation of the contract.

  • Document the agreement in writing whenever possible.

  • Consult a qualified lawyer before concluding contracts of significant financial or legal value.

Syrian law distinguishes, within the framework of the general theory of contract and the special provisions governing certain transactions, between consensual, formal, and real contracts, because each type has different requirements for its formation and the production of its effects.

The general rule is that a contract is based on consent; however, this does not prevent the legislator from requiring a particular form, registration, or delivery whenever protection of the contracting parties or third parties, or stability in transactions, so requires.

Therefore, verifying the nature of a contract before concluding it, and determining whether it is consensual, formal, or real, is an essential step in protecting rights, avoiding disputes, and ensuring that the transaction produces its intended legal effects.

Professional Notice

This article is intended to provide a general educational legal overview of the provisions governing consensual, formal, and real contracts under Syrian law. It does not constitute specific legal advice or a final professional opinion in a particular case. The legal outcome may vary according to the facts, the wording of the contract, the nature of the transaction, the applicable special provisions, and relevant judicial precedent. It is therefore advisable to consult a qualified lawyer before concluding any contract or taking any legal action with a significant financial or legal effect.

References

blogs.titleEn: Defects of Consent in Syrian Law: Mistake, Duress, Fraud, and Exploitation
blogs.excerptEn: Free will and sound consent are fundamental to contracts under Syrian civil law. A contract may be rescinded where consent is impaired by mistake, duress, fraud, or exploitation.
blogs.seoTitleEn: Defects of Consent in Syrian Law
blogs.seoDescriptionEn: Learn how mistake, duress, fraud, and exploitation affect contractual consent and rescission under Syrian civil law.
blogs.bodyEn:
Introduction: The Nature of Defects of Consent and Their Effect on Contract Validity

Defects of consent are circumstances or means that affect the will of one of the contracting parties when entering into a contract, causing that party to agree to the contract when, absent those circumstances, the party would not have entered into it or would not have accepted it on the same terms.

These defects do not render the contract non-existent; rather, they make it voidable for the benefit of the party whose will is affected by them.

Part One: Defects of Consent Affecting Consent

Section One: Mistake

Mistake is an incorrect perception of reality that induces a person to enter into a contract.

A mistake occurs when a contracting party believes something untrue, and that belief is the principal reason for accepting the contract.

Examples of Mistake

·       Purchasing a painting believing it to be original, only to discover that it is a counterfeit.

·       Purchasing land on the basis that it is suitable for construction, only to discover that it is classified as an agricultural zone where construction is prohibited.

·       Purchasing an industrial machine in the belief that it is new when it is used.

Not every mistake is sufficient to rescind a contract; it must be a material mistake that affects the contracting party’s consent, such that the party would not have entered into the contract had the truth been known.

Section Two: Duress

Duress is unlawful pressure exerted on a person that induces that person to contract out of fear of serious harm befalling them or one of their relatives.

Duress need not be physical only; it may also be psychological.

Examples of Duress

·       Threatening to harm a family member.

·       Threatening to unlawfully disclose private information.

·       Forcing a person to sign a contract under threat of force.

The fear caused by duress must be serious enough to affect a reasonable person and induce that person to sign.

Ordinary commercial pressure or difficult negotiations, however, do not constitute duress in the legal sense.

Section Three: Fraud

Fraud is the use of deceptive means, the provision of false information, or the concealment of material facts with the intention of inducing the other party to contract.

Fraud is not established by mere simple lying; rather, the deception must affect the contracting party’s will.

Examples of Fraud

·       Falsifying financial data to persuade an investor to purchase a company.

·       Concealing the existence of litigation relating to the property being sold.

·       Altering a vehicle’s odometer to display fewer kilometres than the actual figure.

·       Submitting forged documents to establish ownership of, or the suitability of, a product.

Once fraud is established, the injured party has the right to seek rescission of the contract and claim compensation where the conditions for liability are met.

Section Four: Exploitation

Exploitation is where one contracting party takes advantage of the other party’s state of weakness, need, recklessness, or overpowering passion to obtain an unfair benefit.

Exploitation differs from fraud: the exploiting party may neither lie nor deceive, but instead benefits from the other party’s circumstances to obtain an excessive gain.

Examples of Exploitation

·       Purchasing real property from a person in financial distress for a price far below its true value.

·       Lending to a person in need in exchange for unfair interest or terms.

·       Taking advantage of one contracting party’s lack of experience to include grossly unbalanced terms.

In this case, depending on the circumstances of the action, the judge may rescind the contract or amend the obligations so as to eliminate unfairness and exploitation in accordance with the law.

Part Two: Comparison of Defects of Consent

Defect - Cause of the Defect - Means

Mistake - Incorrect perception of reality - Error in belief

Duress - Threat or unlawful pressure - Fear

Fraud - Deception, lying, or concealment of the truth - Deceit

Exploitation - Taking advantage of the contracting party’s weakness - Gross imbalance

Part Three: Legal Effects of Defects of Consent

If the existence of a defect of consent is established before the court, the contract is not automatically void; rather, it is voidable at the request of the party whose will was affected by that defect.

Depending on the nature of the dispute, the injured party may seek:

·       Rescission of the contract.

·       Restoration of the contracting parties to the position they were in before contracting.

·       Compensation for damage suffered, where the elements of civil liability are present.

·       Repayment of sums or property delivered in performance of the contract.

Part Four: Proving Defects of Consent Before the Courts

The burden of proving mistake, duress, fraud, or exploitation rests on the person relying on it before the courts. Various legally admissible means of evidence may be relied upon, including:

·       Electronic correspondence.

·       Text messages.

·       Recordings permitted by law.

·       Witnesses.

·       Technical reports and expert evidence.

·       Judicial presumptions.

Part Five: The Importance of Legal Review Before Contracting

Many contractual disputes arise from hastily signing contracts without legally reviewing them or verifying the accuracy of information supplied by the other party.

It is therefore always advisable to:

·       Read all clauses carefully.

·       Verify documents and information.

·       Not sign under any pressure.

·       Seek the assistance of a lawyer before entering into contracts of significant financial or legal value.

Conclusion

The protection of free will is one of the fundamental principles on which Syrian civil law is based. The law does not merely require a signature or an exchange of offer and acceptance; it requires consent to arise from an informed, sound will free from mistake, duress, fraud, and exploitation.

Understanding these provisions is not limited to lawyers; it is an important safeguard for every individual or company before entering into any contractual relationship, and it contributes to reducing disputes, protecting rights, and achieving stability in civil and commercial transactions.

blogs.bodyEn:
Electronic Contracts in the Saudi Legal System

Their Evidentiary Value and Methods of Proof Before the Courts

Learn about the evidentiary value of electronic contracts in the Saudi legal system, the requirements for a valid electronic signature, and the means of proving digital contracts before the courts, together with the key practical recommendations for parties and electronic platforms to ensure sound contracting and protect rights.

Introduction:

In the age of digital transformation, electronic contracts have become an essential part of commercial transactions in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. With the expanding use of electronic platforms and smart applications, a fundamental question has emerged: Do electronic contracts have evidentiary value before Saudi courts? And how can they be proven in the event of a dispute?

This article offers a precise yet accessible legal reading that combines statutory analysis and judicial direction, suitable for specialists and the general public.

Notice: This article is for general legal education purposes and does not constitute legal advice or replace consultation with a specialist based on the facts of each case.

First: The nature of the electronic contract.

An electronic contract is an agreement concluded through an electronic means, whether through:

  • E-commerce platforms

  • Email

  • Text messages

  • Smart applications

  • Approved electronic contracting systems

An electronic contract has recognised legal effect when its statutory elements and conditions are met and the means of concluding and preserving it can be verified and attributed to its parties.

Second: The statutory basis for electronic contracts in Saudi Arabia.

The evidentiary value of electronic contracts is based on several laws, most notably:

  • Electronic Transactions Law

  • Anti-Cybercrime Law

  • Civil Transactions Law

·         Relevant judicial applications

These laws confirm that electronic contracting is valid and enforceable provided that:

  • Consent is established

  • Electronic identity is authenticated

  • Data are preserved securely

  • The contract can be attributed to its parties

Third: The elements of the electronic contract.

1) Electronic consent:

It is established through:

  • Clicking an acceptance button

  • Sending a message of acceptance

  • Electronic signature

  • Actually performing the obligation after receiving the offer

2) Subject matter:

It must be lawful and specified, whether it is a good, service, or financial right.

3) Cause:

It must be lawful and not contrary to the laws.

Fourth: The evidentiary value of the electronic signature.

The electronic signature is one of the most important elements for proving electronic contracts, and it is valid if it is:

  • Issued by a trusted entity

  • Linked to its owner in a manner that cannot be repudiated

  • Not capable of being altered without a clear trace

  • Approved by the Digital Government Authority or a trusted service provider

An electronic signature has recognised evidentiary value when it meets the statutory and technical requirements that ensure identification of the signatory, the integrity of the document, and the ability to detect any subsequent alteration.

Fifth: Methods of proving electronic contracts before the courts.

Saudi courts rely on the following electronic evidence:

  • Electronic platform records

  • Email

  • Text messages

  • Electronic payment records

  • Electronic signature

  • Approved digital records

  • Electronic system logs (Logs)

  • Certificates from technical service providers

This evidence has recognised evidentiary value if it is:

  • Clear

  • Capable of attribution

  • Not susceptible to tampering

  • Issued by a trusted system

Sixth: The principal disputes relating to electronic contracts.

Common disputes include:

  • Denial of contracting

  • Denial of electronic identity

  • Non-conformity of the good or service

  • Delay in performance

  • Failure to comply with platform terms

  • Electronic fraud

Saudi courts tend to protect the good-faith party, particularly where the platform is trusted and maintains accurate records.

Seventh: Liability of electronic platforms.

Platforms bear statutory responsibilities, including:

  • Preserving records

  • Authenticating identity

  • Protecting data

  • Providing a clear record of transactions

  • Complying with technical and security requirements

A platform may be held accountable for any technical defect that causes harm to a party.

Eighth: Practical recommendations for merchants and electronic transactors.

To ensure strong legal protection, the following are recommended:

  • Use trusted platforms

  • Retain contracting and payment records

  • Use an approved electronic signature

  • Document commercial correspondence

  • Read the platform terms before contracting

  • Seek assistance from a legal adviser for major contracts

Electronic contracts have become a commercial and regulatory reality that cannot be ignored. Saudi law grants them recognised evidentiary value when their elements and requirements are satisfied and they can be attributed to and verified against their parties. The more thoroughly the data are documented, identities authenticated, and records securely preserved, the stronger the electronic contract becomes before the courts and the less likely disputes are over its validity or attribution to its parties.

Frequently Asked Questions About Electronic Contracts.

Is an electronic contract legally binding?

Yes, when it satisfies its elements and statutory requirements and its issuance by its parties can be proven.

Is email sufficient to prove contracting?

Email may be recognised evidence if it clearly indicates offer and acceptance and can be attributed to its sender and its integrity verified.

What are the strongest means of proving an electronic contract?

Among the strongest are an authenticated electronic signature, platform records, payment records, electronic system logs, and certificates from technical service providers.

Does an electronic signature replace a handwritten signature?

Yes, an electronic signature can take the place of a handwritten signature when it meets the statutory and technical requirements that establish the signatory's identity, the document's integrity, and the ability to verify it.

blogs.seoDescriptionEn: A practical guide to the elements, validity requirements, formation stages, and legal consequences of commercial contracts under Saudi law.
blogs.bodyEn:
Formation of Commercial Contracts Under Saudi Law

Elements, Requirements, and Consequences of Their Absence

A commercial contract is the cornerstone of economic transactions within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It is the framework upon which obligations and rights between parties are established and serves as a legal reference when a dispute arises. With the expansion of commercial activity and the diversity of contractual arrangements, it has become essential to understand how a contract is formed, the requirements for its validity, and the consequences arising from the absence of any of its elements.

First: The Nature and Importance of a Commercial Contract.

A commercial contract is an agreement that creates reciprocal obligations between two or more parties and is intended to achieve a commercial purpose, such as supply, contracting, agency, franchise, or other transactions.
The importance of a contract lies in its being:

  • A means of protecting commercial rights

  • An instrument for regulating the relationship between the parties

  • A judicial reference in the event of a dispute

  • A safeguard for the stability of market transactions

Second: Elements of Formation of a Commercial Contract Under Saudi Law.

A contract is not formed unless three principal elements are present:

1) Mutual Consent (Offer and Acceptance):

This is the meeting of two wills to create an obligation.
Mutual consent is established through:

  • Commercial negotiations

  • Offers made

  • Express or implied acceptance

  • Electronic and written correspondence

Saudi courts attach significant evidentiary value to commercial correspondence, particularly where it includes clear acceptance or actual performance.

2) Subject Matter (Object of the Contract):

The subject matter must be:

  • Lawful

  • Possible

  • Specified or capable of being specified

Accordingly, a contract concerning an unknown or unlawful matter is invalid or voidable.

3) Cause (the Lawful Purpose of the Contract):

The cause is the lawful purpose for which the contract was concluded, and it must be lawful and not contrary to laws or public morals.

Third: Requirements for the Validity of a Commercial Contract.

In addition to the basic elements, the validity of a contract requires:

  • Capacity of the parties: each party must have the capacity to contract.

  • Absence of defects in consent: such as mistake, duress, fraud, or exploitation.

  • Writing: it is not always a requirement for the validity of a contract, but it is a requirement for proof in most commercial transactions.

  • Precise definition of obligations: to avoid disputes relating to interpretation or performance.

Fourth: Stages of Formation of a Commercial Contract.

A commercial contract generally passes through four main stages:

  • Negotiation stage: exchange of information and offers.

  • Offer stage: submission of a clear and definite offer.

  • Acceptance stage: the other party's acceptance of the offer without amendment.

  • Documentation stage: recording and signing the contract, or proving it through approved electronic means.

Electronic correspondence and messages transmitted through commercial platforms have recognized evidentiary value before Saudi courts.

Fifth: Consequences of the Absence of an Element or Requirement of the Contract.

Where an element or requirement is absent, the consequences vary according to the nature of the defect:

  • Invalidity of the contract: where a fundamental element, such as the subject matter or mutual consent, is absent.

  • Voidability of the contract: where consent is affected by a defect.

  • Unenforceability of the contract: where one of the parties lacks capacity to contract.

  • Termination of the contract: where one party breaches its obligations after the contract has been validly formed.

Commercial courts tend to protect the good-faith party and restore contractual balance where there is a breach or clear unfairness.

Sixth: Practical Recommendations for Traders When Drafting Contracts.

To avoid disputes and achieve the highest degree of legal protection, traders are advised to:

  • Document every stage of negotiation

  • Define obligations precisely and clearly

  • Include a liquidated damages clause in the event of breach

  • Use written contracts instead of oral agreements

  • Seek the assistance of legal counsel when drafting large or complex contracts

The formation of a commercial contract is not merely a formal process; it is an integrated legal structure based on mutual consent, subject matter, and cause. For this structure to be valid, obligations must be clear and consent must be free from defects. The clearer, more written, and more specific the contract is, the lower the likelihood of disputes and the greater the protection afforded to the parties before the courts.

blogs.seoDescriptionEn: Learn how Syrian law requires contracts to be performed in good faith, supporting fair dealing, cooperation, and contractual balance.
blogs.bodyEn:
Performance of Contracts in Good Faith under Syrian Law

A Legal Safeguard for Transactional Stability and Contractual Justice

The stage of contract performance is the real practical test of the contractual relationship; it is where obligations move from written drafting into the reality of dealings between the parties. Disputes often arise not from the terms of the contract itself, but from how one contracting party acts when performing its obligations or exercising its contractual rights.

This is where the importance of the principle of good faith emerges, as a binding legal rule that does not merely require contracting parties to comply with what is expressly stated in the contract, but also requires them to perform their obligations in a manner consistent with integrity, cooperation, and the lawful purpose on which the contract was based.

This article addresses the concept of performing contracts in good faith under Syrian law, its effect on the interpretation and performance of contracts, its principal practical applications, and its relationship to abuse of rights and the burden of proving its breach.

What is meant by performing a contract in good faith?

Good faith in contract performance means that each party must act with integrity, honesty, and cooperation, so that it does not merely perform the obligation formally, but performs it in a way that achieves the lawful purpose intended by the contracting parties.

Accordingly, the obligation of good faith is not confined to the literal meaning of contractual clauses; it extends to what the nature of the obligation, custom, and the requirements of justice demand, preventing harm to the other party or the exploitation of contractual loopholes to secure unlawful gains.

Legal basis:

The Syrian Civil Code enshrines this principle in a clear provision stating:

“A contract must be performed in accordance with its contents and in a manner consistent with the requirements of good faith.”

This provision is a general rule applicable to various civil and commercial contracts, unless a special provision provides otherwise.

What does the principle of good faith require of contracting parties?

The principle of good faith imposes conduct-related obligations inherent in contract performance, most notably:

  • Cooperation between the parties to achieve the purpose of the contract.

  • Refraining from any act that obstructs contract performance without lawful justification.

  • Providing material information that affects performance of the obligation.

  • Avoiding abuse of contractual rights.

  • Preserving the balance on which the contract was based.

Good faith thus becomes an objective legal standard for assessing the conduct of contracting parties, rather than a mere moral directive or general ethical rule.

Good faith does not mean relinquishing rights:

It is a misconception that good faith requires an injured party to be lenient about or waive its rights.

The correct position is that good faith does not prevent a contracting party from claiming its rights or resorting to the courts; rather, it restricts the manner in which those rights are exercised, so that they do not become a means of harming the other party or obtaining an unlawful benefit.

Claiming a lawful right is one thing; abusing it is another.

Practical applications of the principle of good faith:

First: construction contracts.

If technical circumstances arise during performance that require changing the method of work, good faith requires exchanging the necessary information and cooperating to reach an appropriate solution, rather than exploiting the situation to obstruct the project or impose unjustified burdens on the other party.

Second: supply contracts.

If the supplier knows of a delay beyond its control, good faith requires it to notify the buyer immediately and enable the buyer to take the necessary measures to mitigate the damage, rather than concealing the information until the consequences worsen.

Third: lease contracts.

Good faith requires both the lessor and the lessee to cooperate in performing the contract; the lessor may not obstruct the lessee’s enjoyment of the leased property, and the lessee may not use the leased property in a manner contrary to the agreed purpose or causing harm to the lessor.

Fourth: company contracts.

In company contracts, good faith requires partners to disclose material facts affecting the company’s interest and to refrain from exploiting inside information to achieve personal interests at the expense of the company or the other partners.

When is a party deemed to be acting in bad faith?

The court infers bad faith from the circumstances of each case and the conduct of the contracting party during performance. The principal indicators include:

  • Intentional refusal to perform an obligation without lawful cause.

  • Obstructing contract performance to obtain additional gains.

  • Exploiting ambiguity in a contractual clause in a manner contrary to the purpose of the contract.

  • Concealing material information affecting performance.

  • Providing incorrect information during contract performance.

  • Exercising a contractual right with the intention of harming the other party.

In these cases, contractual liability may arise for the breaching party once it is established that its conduct caused harm to the other party.

Effect of good faith on contract interpretation:

The effect of good faith is not limited to the performance stage; it also extends to the interpretation of contractual clauses where there is ambiguity or multiple possible meanings.

If a provision permits more than one interpretation, the interpretation that achieves the lawful purpose of the contract and preserves the balance between the parties takes precedence over an interpretation that leads to an arbitrary or unreasonable result.

The relationship between good faith and abuse of rights:

Good faith is closely connected to the prohibition of abuse of rights. It is not enough for a right to be established by the contract; it must be exercised within limits consistent with its lawful purpose.

A party may have a right provided for under the contract, but exercising it with the intention of harming the other party or securing an unlawful benefit may render that exercise abusive and give rise to liability.

Therefore, when hearing contractual disputes, the courts do not stop at the existence of the right or the contractual provision; they also consider how it was exercised and the extent to which the contracting party’s conduct is consistent with the requirements of integrity, cooperation, and the lawful purpose of the contract.

Burden of proof:

As a general rule, the burden of proving a breach of the principle of good faith lies with the party alleging that breach.

The court may rely on a range of evidence and indicia in forming its conviction, including:

  • Email correspondence.

  • Warnings and notices.

  • Meeting minutes.

  • Change orders.

  • Technical reports.

  • Witness testimony.

  • The parties’ conduct during contract performance.

This evidence is assessed as a whole to determine the true nature of the disputed conduct and whether it is consistent with, or contrary to, the requirements of good faith.

How can disputes relating to contract performance be avoided?

To reduce disputes related to contract performance, it is advisable to observe the following:

  • Draft obligations clearly and precisely.

  • Document all correspondence and subsequent agreements.

  • Give immediate notice of any circumstance affecting performance.

  • Keep a record of all procedures and documents.

  • Address disagreements in their early stages before they escalate.

  • Have contracts reviewed by a legal specialist when amending or performing them.

This means…

Performing a contract in good faith is not an abstract moral principle, but a binding legal rule in the Syrian Civil Code. It requires contracting parties to perform their obligations with integrity and cooperation, in a manner that achieves the lawful purpose of the contract and preserves the balance between rights and obligations.

The importance of this principle lies in moving the contractual relationship beyond mere literal compliance with the text to a broader obligation of lawful conduct, thereby preventing abuse and strengthening trust in transactions.

Accordingly, observing good faith from the negotiation stage until performance is complete is an essential safeguard for the stability of transactions, reducing the likelihood of disputes, and entrenching contractual justice between the parties.

Note: This article is intended for general legal awareness and does not replace specialized legal advice regarding practical facts or existing disputes.

work.titleEn: From a Complex Financial Accusation to a Final Acquittal
work.summaryEn: This matter concerns a financial accusation made against a client because funds were transferred to his personal account …14696 tokens truncated… he worked for a company. **CounselO** conducted a comprehensive legal and accounting review of the file and established that the accounting report alone was insufficient to prove liability and that relevant documents, authorizations, and releases had not been considered. Following an integrated defense strategy, the client was acquitted; the judgment was then affirmed on appeal and became final after affirmation by the Supreme Court.
work.challengeEn:
**The issue:**  
The client was accused of mismanaging the funds of the company for which he worked after financial transfers to his personal account were identified. The company based its accusation on a certified accountant’s report and bank statements, claimed substantial sums, and also initiated criminal proceedings against him.
**The challenge:**  
The principal challenge was that the documents appeared on their face to establish direct financial liability on the client, particularly because the transfers were made to his personal account. The substance of the case was more complex, however: it was necessary to prove that the transfers were not unlawful, explain their relationship to the authorizations, documents, releases, and the company’s operating circumstances, and expose the deficiencies in the accounting report and the evidence submitted by the claimant.
work.approachEn: We conducted an integrated legal and accounting review of the file, beginning with the accusations, accounting report, and bank statements. We then analyzed the financial transfers and connected them to the documents, authorizations, releases, and the company’s operating circumstances. We also exposed shortcomings in the evidence submitted, reconstructed the chronology of events, and developed a comprehensive, document-supported defense strategy. This contributed to the client’s acquittal and its affirmation until the judgment became final.
work.outcomeEn:
**CounselO** achieved a decisive result: the client was acquitted of the financial accusation, the judgment was affirmed on appeal, and it became final after affirmation by the Supreme Court.
The value delivered lay in transforming a file that appeared to establish direct financial liability into an integrated legal and accounting defense by analyzing the evidence, exposing deficiencies in the accounting report, highlighting influential documents, and placing the facts in chronological order—completely changing the course of the case.
work.seoTitleEn: Complex Financial Accusation to Final Acquittal
work.seoDescriptionEn: CounselO built an integrated legal and accounting defense that secured a client’s final acquittal from a complex financial accusation.

work.titleEn: When the First Judgment Is Not the End: How CounselO Reversed an Employment Dispute
work.summaryEn: **CounselO successfully reversed the course of an employment case in which the first-instance court had dismissed the claim. We reanalyzed the file and built a new legal theory based on the continuation of the employment relationship despite the transfer of the establishment’s ownership and the change in its legal form. Connecting the evidence with a judicial admission helped establish the worker’s rights, leading to the reversal of the first-instance judgment and an award of the worker’s entitlements.**
work.challengeEn:
**The issue:**  
The issue was whether a first-instance judgment dismissing an employment claim could be overturned despite indications that the employment relationship continued and the business transferred from one owner to another without any actual interruption.

**The challenge:**  
The evidence submitted appeared fragmented and insufficient on its own. There was no employment contract covering the full period of service, and the establishment’s name and legal form had changed. The case therefore had to be reconstructed, with the facts and evidence connected through a single legal theory establishing the continuation of the employment relationship.
work.approachEn: At CounselO, we reviewed the file of an employment case in which the first-instance court had dismissed the claim, then reanalyzed the facts and evidence and rebuilt the legal theory from the ground up. The work focused on proving that the employment relationship continued despite the transfer of the establishment’s ownership and the change in its legal form by connecting the fragmented evidence and making use of the judicial admission. On that basis, an appellate brief was prepared that led to reversal of the first-instance judgment and an award of the worker’s entitlements.
work.outcomeEn: We legally reconstructed the case after it was lost at first instance by analyzing the facts and evidence and connecting them to Saudi labor law. This led to reversal of the first-instance judgment and a successful appeal for the worker.
work.seoTitleEn: How CounselO Reversed an Employment Dispute
work.seoDescriptionEn: CounselO rebuilt an employment case, proved continuity of employment, overturned the first judgment, and secured the worker’s entitlements.

work.titleEn: Study of an Appeal Before the Supreme Administrative Court
work.summaryEn: A compensation claim that had been ruled inadmissible was reopened. The legal study demonstrated that the compensation claim differed from the earlier claim for contractual entitlements and had not previously been decided. The Supreme Administrative Court accordingly overturned the judgment and remanded the case for reconsideration.
work.challengeEn: The challenge was to prove that the compensation claim was not a repetition of an earlier dispute but an independent right on which the court had never ruled.
work.approachEn: CounselO reviewed the file and analyzed the judgments and documents, identifying the legal error in treating the compensation claim as a repetition of an earlier action. It provided a legal opinion explaining the independent nature of the compensation claim and the absence of any prior adjudication. This helped shape the appeal that resulted in the judgment being overturned and the case being reconsidered.
work.seoDescriptionEn: CounselO showed that a compensation claim was independent, helping overturn the judgment and return the case for reconsideration.
